name: Boron
lead: Boron (symbol B, atomic number 5) is a metalloid element that occurs in nature combined with oxygen in borate minerals and is essential to plant cell-wall formation [1][2][7]. For people, boron is a trace element found in fruit, vegetables, nuts and legumes, and it is sold as a supplement typically as boric acid, calcium fructoborate or boron citrate. It is generally not classed as an essential human nutrient, although it is considered by some authors to be beneficial, and the US Dietary Reference Intakes report of 2001 addressed it among trace elements [15].

In bone-focused and bodybuilding circles, boron is discussed for its proposed effects on calcium, magnesium and vitamin D metabolism and on sex-hormone levels. T Nation forum users in testosterone-therapy threads frequently mention it as a way to influence free testosterone and sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG). A 2008 review found a lack of systematic study of boron's safety and effectiveness in humans, while a 2015 review argues it is important for bone, wound healing, hormone and vitamin D use and inflammation [4][3].

High exposures can be toxic: reviews describe fatalities from boric acid after ingestion or skin exposure and reproductive toxicity in animals [8]. No published study has tested boron for changing facial or jaw bone structure.

paras: Boron-based topical products have been trialled for wound healing: a randomised, double-blind trial tested a sodium pentaborate gel on diabetic foot ulcers, and a phase 3 randomised placebo-controlled trial tested a boron-based gel to prevent radiation dermatitis in breast cancer patients [10][11][19][16]. Separately, boron neutron capture therapy (BNCT) is an experimental radiotherapy that delivers boron-10 compounds to tumours before neutron irradiation [5][6].

Boron appears in supplement stacks for bone, joint comfort and hormone support. A clinical-support review in 2008 discussed nine indications reached through popular use: hormone regulation, cognitive function, osteoarthritis, osteoporosis, topical treatment of vaginitis, bodybuilding (increasing testosterone), menopausal symptoms, anticoagulation effects and topical treatment of psoriasis [4]. No study has examined boron for facial bone or other cosmetic skeletal change.

The 2008 review concluded that systematic study of boron's safety and effectiveness in humans was lacking, despite supportive scientific data for the listed uses [4]. A 2015 review argued that boron is important for bone growth and maintenance, wound healing, the body's use of oestrogen, testosterone and vitamin D, magnesium absorption, inflammatory markers such as hs-CRP and TNF-alpha, antioxidant enzymes, and brain electrical activity and cognition in older adults [3]. These claims are drawn from a mix of small human studies, animal and laboratory data.

The reviews rest on small trials and observational reports rather than large randomised trials of supplements in healthy adults, and the evidence on testosterone is described in more detail under Claims and evidence.
Controlled human research on boron supplements for bone or hormones is sparse in the research record. The 2008 and 2015 reviews summarise small studies and mechanistic data [4][3].

Randomised trials of boron compounds address topical or procedural uses: a sodium pentaborate gel for diabetic foot ulcers [10][16], a boron-based gel for radiation dermatitis in 257 registered participants [11][19], and a randomised phase 2 trial of BNCT for recurrent high-grade meningioma [9]. Registered studies also cover BNCT in head and neck cancer, melanoma, glioblastoma and malignant brain tumours [17][18][20][23][24][25], a diet study comparing boron-rich and Mediterranean diets for gut microbiota and metabolic health [21], and boron levels in periodontitis [22]. Early BNCT work with sodium borocaptate in glioblastoma dates from 1997 [12].
No cited trial tests boron supplementation for testosterone, SHBG, jaw or facial bone outcomes.

A 2021 toxicology review found that boron from food is absorbed in the gastrointestinal tract and excreted mainly in urine, that intact skin is a more effective barrier than compromised skin, and that fatalities have occurred after ingestion and after skin exposure to boric acid; animal endpoints include weight loss and reproductive toxicity, and an animal inhalation study reported reduced foetal weight [8]. The review found that boron compounds are not genotoxic and that boric acid was not carcinogenic in a two-year mouse study [8]. Typical food intake is considered safe, high supplemental doses can cause nausea, diarrhoea and other signs of toxicity, and authorities have set an upper intake level; because of reproductive and developmental concerns, supplements are generally advised against in pregnancy without medical advice [15].

Proposed mechanisms in humans include effects on the metabolism of calcium, magnesium and vitamin D, modulation of steroid hormone levels and inflammatory markers, and influence on biomolecules such as S-adenosyl methionine and NAD+ [3]. The mechanisms are not well established in humans [4]. In plants, boron is implicated in cell-wall structure, membrane function and metabolism, although its primary biochemical role remains unclear [7].

Boron is a low-abundance metalloid (about 0.001 percent of Earth's crust by weight) that occurs as borate minerals such as borax and kernite, with Turkey the largest producer [1]. Boric acid and borates are used in glass, ceramics, detergents, fertilisers, fire retardants and wood preservatives [1][2]. Boron nitride and other boron nanomaterials are also studied in materials science [13][14].

Borax, in its mineral form tincal, was used as a glaze from about 300 AD in China, and boric acid was recognised in Italian hot springs in 1777, when it was known as sal sedativum with ostensible medical benefits [1]. Humphry Davy observed in 1808 that electric current through a borate solution deposited a brown precipitate, and he named the new element boracium; Gay-Lussac and Thenard obtained boron independently, and Berzelius identified it as an element in 1824 [1].

Boron became prominent in strength-sport and testosterone-therapy forums, notably in a 2019 T Nation thread titled 'Boron - All My Patients Use It and So Should You', which ran to more than 250 posts [31]. Users in other threads on testosterone therapy, SHBG and lab results ask whether boron changed their numbers, and some report taking it as part of a stack that includes zinc, magnesium, vitamin D or DHEA [28][30][32][34]. Others say a doctor recommended it for joint pain [26].

lore.intro: On T Nation, boron is discussed mainly by men on testosterone therapy or with high SHBG, who treat it as an inexpensive supplement for raising free testosterone, and secondarily as a joint and bone aid [31][28][26].

claims.claim: Boron raises free testosterone and lowers SHBG
claims.believers: Posters say boron is shown to help with free testosterone, and a thread titled 'Boron - All My Patients Use It and So Should You' presents it as a routine supplement for patients; one commenter reports an endocrinologist saying all his TRT patients take it daily [31][27][29]. A clinic-provided regimen for high SHBG listed boron alongside DHEA, ZMA and fish oil [28].
claims.experts: A 2008 clinical-support review lists bodybuilding use to increase testosterone among indications but found a lack of systematic study of boron's effectiveness and safety in humans [4]. A 2015 review argues boron beneficially affects the body's use of oestrogen and testosterone, drawing on a mix of study types [3].

claims.claim: Most people are boron deficient, so supplementing is a sensible default
claims.believers: One post recalls a doctor saying nearly everyone is deficient in boron and that taking it raises receptors and free testosterone, and another poster calls most of the population boron deficient and says supplementing is reasonable for health and gym performance [33][34].
claims.experts: Boron is not classed as an essential human nutrient, no deficiency syndrome is defined, and the Dietary Reference Intakes report addressed boron mainly by setting an upper limit [15][4].

claims.claim: Boron-rich foods such as raisins and pomegranate juice can serve as a boron source
claims.believers: A poster in a cancer-recovery thread says raisins are among the highest-boron foods and recommends dried fruit and pomegranate juice for free testosterone [27].
claims.experts: Fruit, vegetables, nuts and legumes are recognised dietary sources of boron [1].

claims.claim: Boron helps joint and bone health
claims.believers: A T Nation member says his doctor suggested boron for joint pain and that he had been taking it earlier in the year [26].
claims.experts: Osteoarthritis and osteoporosis are among indications reviewed in 2008, and a 2015 review says boron is important for growth and maintenance of bone; that 2008 review described the human evidence base as lacking systematic study [4][3].

claims.claim: Boron supplements can cause problems when combined with other supplements in testosterone therapy
claims.believers: A user in a thread about signs that a therapeutic dose is too high speculates that zinc, boron and other supplements caused libido and erection problems during testosterone therapy, while noting the regimen was not dialled in [32].
claims.experts: No controlled studies of boron combined with testosterone therapy appear in the published research cited here; toxicology reviews describe adverse effects mainly at high exposures [8].
